turns.assistant:
Gravitational lensing does bend every photon, but the amount depends on the mass that the light passes near.  
The deflection angle for a body of mass \(M\) at closest approach distance \(b\) is  

\[
\theta \approx \frac{4GM}{c^{2}b}.
\]

For Earth ( \(M≈6×10^{24}\) kg) and a ray that just grazes the surface (\(b≈R_{\oplus}=6.4×10^{6}\) m),

\[
\theta \approx 2.8×10^{-9}\ \text{rad} \approx 0.6\ \text{mas}.
\]

Even the Sun, the most massive nearby object, bends starlight by only ~1.75 arcseconds at its limb.  
Telescopes on Earth have angular resolutions of a few tens of milliarcseconds at best, and atmospheric “seeing” blurs images by ~1 arcsecond.  

Thus the gravitational distortion produced by Earth, Mars, Jupiter, etc., is many orders of magnitude smaller than what any current telescope can resolve, so the planets appear undistorted.
